\author{Wisest Maths --- Year 1 A-Level, Integration (ref \texttt{i1})}

\begin{document}
\maketitle
\noindent This document contains all 70 \emph{Indefinite Integration} questions, each with a
fully worked solution and a TikZ graph. Because an indefinite integral is only determined up to a constant, each
diagram shows the \emph{family of antiderivative curves} \(y=F(x)+C\) (grey, vertical translates of one another),
with one representative member drawn in blue. For the questions with a boundary condition, the particular curve is
highlighted and the given point is marked --- showing how the condition fixes the value of \(C\).
\tableofcontents
\bigskip
\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 01\quad\small\texttt{(i1-001)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 01 (i1-001)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 1}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int x^6 \, \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Apply the integration power rule: increase the index by 1 and divide by the new index.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int x^6 \, \mathrm{d}x = \frac{x^7}{7} + C
\end{gathered}\]
The rule is \( \displaystyle\int x^n \, \mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C \). Here \( n = 6 \), so the index becomes 7.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  \dfrac{x^7}{7} + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 02\quad\small\texttt{(i1-002)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 02 (i1-002)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 1}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int 5x^4 \, \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Take the constant outside the integral, then integrate.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int 5x^4 \, \mathrm{d}x = 5 \cdot \frac{x^5}{5} + C = x^5 + C
\end{gathered}\]
The constant 5 multiplies the integral. Increase the index from 4 to 5 and divide by 5; the 5s cancel.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  x^5 + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 03\quad\small\texttt{(i1-003)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 03 (i1-003)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 1}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int 8x \, \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Write \( 8x = 8x^1 \) and apply the power rule.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int 8x \, \mathrm{d}x = 8 \cdot \frac{x^2}{2} + C = 4x^2 + C
\end{gathered}\]
Increase the index from 1 to 2 and divide by 2; \( 8 \div 2 = 4 \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  4x^2 + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 04\quad\small\texttt{(i1-004)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 04 (i1-004)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 1}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int 12 \, \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Write 12 as \( 12x^0 \) and integrate.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int 12 \, \mathrm{d}x = 12x + C
\end{gathered}\]
Integrating a constant \( k \) gives \( kx + C \). The index increases from 0 to 1 and we divide by 1.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  12x + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\small The family of antiderivative curves \(y=F(x)+C\) --- vertical translates differing by the constant \(C\).\normalsize

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 05\quad\small\texttt{(i1-005)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 05 (i1-005)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 1}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int -3x^2 \, \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Apply the power rule with the negative constant.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int -3x^2 \, \mathrm{d}x = -3 \cdot \frac{x^3}{3} + C = -x^3 + C
\end{gathered}\]
Increase the index from 2 to 3 and divide by 3; \( -3 \div 3 = -1 \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  -x^3 + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Indefinite Integration 06\quad\small\texttt{(i1-006)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 06 (i1-006)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 2}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int x^{-3} \, \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Apply the power rule with \( n = -3 \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int x^{-3} \, \mathrm{d}x = \frac{x^{-2}}{-2} + C = -\frac{1}{2x^2} + C
\end{gathered}\]
Increase the index from \(-3\) to \(-2\) and divide by \(-2\).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  -\dfrac{1}{2x^2} + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\node[blue!72!black,scale=0.72,fill=white,inner sep=1pt] at (4.1,5.548) {$y=-\frac{1}{2x^2}+C$};
\end{tikzpicture}
}
\end{center}
\small The family of antiderivative curves \(y=F(x)+C\) --- vertical translates differing by the constant \(C\).\normalsize

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 07\quad\small\texttt{(i1-007)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 07 (i1-007)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 2}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int \sqrt{x} \, \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Rewrite \( \sqrt{x} = x^{1/2} \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int x^{1/2} \, \mathrm{d}x
\end{gathered}\]
Always convert surds to fractional powers before integrating.

\textit{Step 2: Apply the power rule.}
\[\begin{gathered}
= \frac{x^{3/2}}{3/2} + C = \frac{2}{3}x^{3/2} + C
\end{gathered}\]
Increase the index from \( \tfrac{1}{2} \) to \( \tfrac{3}{2} \) and divide by \( \tfrac{3}{2} \) --- dividing by a fraction is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal.

\textit{Step 3: Rewrite using surd notation if required.}
\[\begin{gathered}
= \frac{2}{3}x\sqrt{x} + C
\end{gathered}\]
\( x^{3/2} = x \cdot \sqrt{x} \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  \dfrac{2}{3}x^{3/2} + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 08\quad\small\texttt{(i1-008)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 08 (i1-008)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 2}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int \frac{4}{x^2} \, \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Rewrite as a negative power of \( x \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int 4x^{-2} \, \mathrm{d}x
\end{gathered}\]
\( \dfrac{4}{x^2} = 4x^{-2} \).

\textit{Step 2: Integrate.}
\[\begin{gathered}
= 4 \cdot \frac{x^{-1}}{-1} + C = -4x^{-1} + C = -\frac{4}{x} + C
\end{gathered}\]
Increase the index from \(-2\) to \(-1\) and divide by \(-1\).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  -\dfrac{4}{x} + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 09\quad\small\texttt{(i1-009)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 09 (i1-009)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 3}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int (3x^2 + 5x - 2) \, \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Integrate each term separately.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int 3x^2 \, \mathrm{d}x + \int 5x \, \mathrm{d}x + \int (-2) \, \mathrm{d}x
\end{gathered}\]
The integral of a sum equals the sum of the integrals.

\textit{Step 2: Apply the power rule to each term.}
\[\begin{gathered}
= 3 \cdot \frac{x^3}{3} + 5 \cdot \frac{x^2}{2} - 2x + C
\end{gathered}\]
Increase each index by 1 and divide by the new index.

\textit{Step 3: Simplify.}
\[\begin{gathered}
= x^3 + \frac{5x^2}{2} - 2x + C
\end{gathered}\]
\( 3 \div 3 = 1 \). Only one constant of integration is needed for the whole expression.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  x^3 + \dfrac{5x^2}{2} - 2x + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 10\quad\small\texttt{(i1-010)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 10 (i1-010)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 3}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int (4x^3 - 6x^2 + 1) \, \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Integrate each term separately.}
\[\begin{gathered}
= 4 \cdot \frac{x^4}{4} - 6 \cdot \frac{x^3}{3} + x + C
\end{gathered}\]
Apply \( \int x^n \, \mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} \) to each term.

\textit{Step 2: Simplify.}
\[\begin{gathered}
= x^4 - 2x^3 + x + C
\end{gathered}\]
\( 4 \div 4 = 1 \) and \( 6 \div 3 = 2 \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  x^4 - 2x^3 + x + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Indefinite Integration 11\quad\small\texttt{(i1-011)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 11 (i1-011)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 3}

\question{Expand and then integrate \( (x + 3)(x - 2) \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Expand the bracket.}
\[\begin{gathered}
(x+3)(x-2) = x^2 + x - 6
\end{gathered}\]
FOIL: \( x^2 - 2x + 3x - 6 \).

\textit{Step 2: Integrate term by term.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int (x^2 + x - 6) \, \mathrm{d}x = \frac{x^3}{3} + \frac{x^2}{2} - 6x + C
\end{gathered}\]
Apply the power rule to each term.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  \dfrac{x^3}{3} + \dfrac{x^2}{2} - 6x + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Indefinite Integration 12\quad\small\texttt{(i1-012)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 12 (i1-012)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 3}

\question{Expand and integrate \( x^2(3x - 5) \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Expand.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x^2(3x - 5) = 3x^3 - 5x^2
\end{gathered}\]
Multiply \( x^2 \) by each term inside the bracket.

\textit{Step 2: Integrate.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int (3x^3 - 5x^2) \, \mathrm{d}x = \frac{3x^4}{4} - \frac{5x^3}{3} + C
\end{gathered}\]
Apply the power rule to each term.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  \dfrac{3x^4}{4} - \dfrac{5x^3}{3} + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Indefinite Integration 13\quad\small\texttt{(i1-013)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 13 (i1-013)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 3}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int (2x - 1)^2 \, \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Expand \( (2x-1)^2 \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
(2x-1)^2 = 4x^2 - 4x + 1
\end{gathered}\]
\( (a-b)^2 = a^2 - 2ab + b^2 \) with \( a = 2x \), \( b = 1 \).

\textit{Step 2: Integrate each term.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int (4x^2 - 4x + 1) \, \mathrm{d}x = \frac{4x^3}{3} - 2x^2 + x + C
\end{gathered}\]
Power rule applied to each term.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  \dfrac{4x^3}{3} - 2x^2 + x + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 14\quad\small\texttt{(i1-014)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 14 (i1-014)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 3}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int \left( x^{1/3} + 2x \right) \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Integrate each term.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int x^{1/3} \, \mathrm{d}x + \int 2x \, \mathrm{d}x
\end{gathered}\]
Integrate term by term.

\textit{Step 2: Apply the power rule.}
\[\begin{gathered}
= \frac{x^{4/3}}{4/3} + x^2 + C = \frac{3}{4}x^{4/3} + x^2 + C
\end{gathered}\]
For \( x^{1/3} \): new index \( = \tfrac{4}{3} \); dividing by \( \tfrac{4}{3} \) gives \( \times \tfrac{3}{4} \). For \( 2x \): \( 2 \cdot \dfrac{x^2}{2} = x^2 \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  \dfrac{3}{4}x^{4/3} + x^2 + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 15\quad\small\texttt{(i1-015)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 15 (i1-015)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 3}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int \frac{x^3 - 4x}{x} \, \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Simplify the fraction by dividing each term by \( x \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
\frac{x^3 - 4x}{x} = x^2 - 4
\end{gathered}\]
\( \dfrac{x^3}{x} = x^2 \) and \( \dfrac{-4x}{x} = -4 \).

\textit{Step 2: Integrate.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int (x^2 - 4) \, \mathrm{d}x = \frac{x^3}{3} - 4x + C
\end{gathered}\]
Power rule applied to \( x^2 \); integrating the constant \(-4\) gives \(-4x\).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  \dfrac{x^3}{3} - 4x + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 16\quad\small\texttt{(i1-016)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 16 (i1-016)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 3}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int \frac{6x^4 + 3x^2}{3x} \, \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Divide each term in the numerator by \( 3x \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
\frac{6x^4}{3x} + \frac{3x^2}{3x} = 2x^3 + x
\end{gathered}\]
\( \dfrac{6x^4}{3x} = 2x^3 \) and \( \dfrac{3x^2}{3x} = x \).

\textit{Step 2: Integrate.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int (2x^3 + x) \, \mathrm{d}x = \frac{x^4}{2} + \frac{x^2}{2} + C
\end{gathered}\]
\( 2 \cdot \dfrac{x^4}{4} = \dfrac{x^4}{2} \) and \( \dfrac{x^2}{2} \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  \dfrac{x^4}{2} + \dfrac{x^2}{2} + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Indefinite Integration 17\quad\small\texttt{(i1-017)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 17 (i1-017)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int \left( 3\sqrt{x} - \frac{2}{x^2} \right) \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Rewrite using index notation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
3x^{1/2} - 2x^{-2}
\end{gathered}\]
\( \sqrt{x} = x^{1/2} \) and \( \dfrac{1}{x^2} = x^{-2} \).

\textit{Step 2: Integrate each term.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int 3x^{1/2} \, \mathrm{d}x - \int 2x^{-2} \, \mathrm{d}x = 3 \cdot \frac{x^{3/2}}{3/2} - 2 \cdot \frac{x^{-1}}{-1} + C
\end{gathered}\]
Apply the power rule to each term.

\textit{Step 3: Simplify.}
\[\begin{gathered}
= 2x^{3/2} + \frac{2}{x} + C
\end{gathered}\]
\( 3 \div \tfrac{3}{2} = 3 \times \tfrac{2}{3} = 2 \). \( -2 \div (-1) = 2 \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  2x^{3/2} + \dfrac{2}{x} + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 18\quad\small\texttt{(i1-018)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 18 (i1-018)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int \sqrt{x}(x + 4) \, \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Expand by multiplying \( x^{1/2} \) through the bracket.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\sqrt{x}(x+4) = x^{3/2} + 4x^{1/2}
\end{gathered}\]
\( x^{1/2} \cdot x = x^{3/2} \) and \( x^{1/2} \cdot 4 = 4x^{1/2} \).

\textit{Step 2: Integrate each term.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int (x^{3/2} + 4x^{1/2}) \, \mathrm{d}x = \frac{x^{5/2}}{5/2} + 4 \cdot \frac{x^{3/2}}{3/2} + C
\end{gathered}\]
Power rule applied to each fractional-index term.

\textit{Step 3: Simplify.}
\[\begin{gathered}
= \frac{2}{5}x^{5/2} + \frac{8}{3}x^{3/2} + C
\end{gathered}\]
Dividing by \( \tfrac{5}{2} \) gives \( \times \tfrac{2}{5} \); dividing by \( \tfrac{3}{2} \) gives \( \times \tfrac{2}{3} \), then \( \times 4 = \tfrac{8}{3} \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  \dfrac{2}{5}x^{5/2} + \dfrac{8}{3}x^{3/2} + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Indefinite Integration 19\quad\small\texttt{(i1-019)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 19 (i1-019)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int \frac{x^2 + 5x + 6}{\sqrt{x}} \, \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Divide each term by \( x^{1/2} \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
x^{3/2} + 5x^{1/2} + 6x^{-1/2}
\end{gathered}\]
\( \dfrac{x^2}{x^{1/2}} = x^{3/2} \), \( \dfrac{5x}{x^{1/2}} = 5x^{1/2} \), \( \dfrac{6}{x^{1/2}} = 6x^{-1/2} \).

\textit{Step 2: Integrate each term.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int (x^{3/2} + 5x^{1/2} + 6x^{-1/2}) \, \mathrm{d}x = \frac{2}{5}x^{5/2} + \frac{10}{3}x^{3/2} + 12x^{1/2} + C
\end{gathered}\]
Apply \( \int x^n \, \mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} \) to each term.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  \dfrac{2}{5}x^{5/2} + \dfrac{10}{3}x^{3/2} + 12\sqrt{x} + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Indefinite Integration 20\quad\small\texttt{(i1-020)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 20 (i1-020)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 3}

\question{Find \( y \) given that \( \dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = 6x^2 - 4x + 3 \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Integrate the right-hand side with respect to \( x \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = \int (6x^2 - 4x + 3) \, \mathrm{d}x
\end{gathered}\]
Integrating \( \dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} \) gives \( y \).

\textit{Step 2: Apply the power rule to each term.}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = 2x^3 - 2x^2 + 3x + C
\end{gathered}\]
\( 6 \cdot \dfrac{x^3}{3} = 2x^3 \), \( 4 \cdot \dfrac{x^2}{2} = 2x^2 \), \( 3x^0 \to 3x \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  y = 2x^3 - 2x^2 + 3x + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Indefinite Integration 21\quad\small\texttt{(i1-021)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 21 (i1-021)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{The curve \( y = f(x) \) passes through the point \( (0, 3) \) and \( f'(x) = 4x - 1 \). Find \( f(x) \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Integrate \( f'(x) \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
f(x) = \int (4x - 1) \, \mathrm{d}x = 2x^2 - x + C
\end{gathered}\]
Power rule applied to each term.

\textit{Step 2: Use the point \( (0, 3) \) to find \( C \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
f(0) = 3: \quad 0 - 0 + C = 3 \implies C = 3
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute \( x = 0 \) and \( f(0) = 3 \).

\textit{Step 3: Write the full equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
f(x) = 2x^2 - x + 3
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute the found value of \( C \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  f(x) = 2x^2 - x + 3 \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 22\quad\small\texttt{(i1-022)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 22 (i1-022)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{A curve passes through \( (2, 5) \) and has gradient function \( f'(x) = 3x^2 - 6x + 1 \). Find \( f(x) \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Integrate the gradient function.}
\[\begin{gathered}
f(x) = \int (3x^2 - 6x + 1) \, \mathrm{d}x = x^3 - 3x^2 + x + C
\end{gathered}\]
Apply the power rule to each term.

\textit{Step 2: Substitute \( (2, 5) \) to find \( C \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
5 = 8 - 12 + 2 + C \implies 5 = -2 + C \implies C = 7
\end{gathered}\]
Replace \( x = 2 \) and \( f(x) = 5 \).

\textit{Step 3: State the equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 + x + 7
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute \( C = 7 \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 + x + 7 \)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Indefinite Integration 23\quad\small\texttt{(i1-023)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 23 (i1-023)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{A curve \( y = f(x) \) passes through \( (1, -2) \) and \( f'(x) = 6x(x - 2) \). Find \( f(x) \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Expand \( f'(x) \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
f'(x) = 6x^2 - 12x
\end{gathered}\]
Multiply \( 6x \) by each term in the bracket.

\textit{Step 2: Integrate.}
\[\begin{gathered}
f(x) = \int (6x^2 - 12x) \, \mathrm{d}x = 2x^3 - 6x^2 + C
\end{gathered}\]
Apply the power rule.

\textit{Step 3: Use the point \( (1, -2) \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
-2 = 2(1) - 6(1) + C = -4 + C \implies C = 2
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute \( x = 1 \), \( f(1) = -2 \).

\textit{Step 4: State the answer.}
\[\begin{gathered}
f(x) = 2x^3 - 6x^2 + 2
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute \( C = 2 \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  f(x) = 2x^3 - 6x^2 + 2 \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 24\quad\small\texttt{(i1-024)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 24 (i1-024)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{The gradient of a curve is given by \( \dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}} \). Given that the curve passes through \( (4, 10) \), find the equation of the curve.}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Rewrite \( \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}} = x^{-1/2} \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = \int x^{-1/2} \, \mathrm{d}x
\end{gathered}\]
Convert to index notation.

\textit{Step 2: Integrate.}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = \frac{x^{1/2}}{1/2} + C = 2\sqrt{x} + C
\end{gathered}\]
Increase index from \(-\tfrac{1}{2}\) to \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) and divide by \(\tfrac{1}{2}\).

\textit{Step 3: Use the point \( (4, 10) \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
10 = 2\sqrt{4} + C = 4 + C \implies C = 6
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute \( x = 4 \), \( y = 10 \).

\textit{Step 4: Write the equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = 2\sqrt{x} + 6
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute \( C = 6 \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  y = 2\sqrt{x} + 6 \)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Indefinite Integration 25\quad\small\texttt{(i1-025)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 25 (i1-025)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 5}

\question{A curve passes through \( (3, 4) \) and has gradient function \( f'(x) = 2x - \dfrac{5}{x^2} \). Find \( f(x) \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Rewrite \( \dfrac{5}{x^2} = 5x^{-2} \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
f'(x) = 2x - 5x^{-2}
\end{gathered}\]
Convert to index notation.

\textit{Step 2: Integrate.}
\[\begin{gathered}
f(x) = x^2 - 5 \cdot \frac{x^{-1}}{-1} + C = x^2 + \frac{5}{x} + C
\end{gathered}\]
Apply the power rule to each term.

\textit{Step 3: Use the point \( (3, 4) \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
4 = 9 + \frac{5}{3} + C \implies C = 4 - 9 - \frac{5}{3} = -5 - \frac{5}{3} = -\frac{20}{3}
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute \( x = 3 \), \( f(3) = 4 \).

\textit{Step 4: State the equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
f(x) = x^2 + \frac{5}{x} - \frac{20}{3}
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute \( C = -\dfrac{20}{3} \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  f(x) = x^2 + \dfrac{5}{x} - \dfrac{20}{3} \)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Indefinite Integration 26\quad\small\texttt{(i1-026)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 26 (i1-026)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{Given that \( \dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t} = \sqrt{t} - 3 \) and \( y = 9 \) when \( t = 4 \), find \( y \) as a function of \( t \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Write \( \sqrt{t} = t^{1/2} \) and integrate.}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = \int (t^{1/2} - 3) \, \mathrm{d}t = \frac{2}{3}t^{3/2} - 3t + C
\end{gathered}\]
Apply the power rule to each term in \( t \).

\textit{Step 2: Use \( y = 9 \) when \( t = 4 \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
9 = \frac{2}{3}(8) - 12 + C = \frac{16}{3} - 12 + C
\end{gathered}\]
\( 4^{3/2} = (\sqrt{4})^3 = 8 \).

\textit{Step 3: Solve for \( C \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
C = 9 - \frac{16}{3} + 12 = 21 - \frac{16}{3} = \frac{63 - 16}{3} = \frac{47}{3}
\end{gathered}\]
Rearrange and simplify.

\textit{Step 4: State \( y \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = \frac{2}{3}t^{3/2} - 3t + \frac{47}{3}
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute \( C = \dfrac{47}{3} \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  y = \dfrac{2}{3}t^{3/2} - 3t + \dfrac{47}{3} \)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Indefinite Integration 27\quad\small\texttt{(i1-027)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 27 (i1-027)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 5}

\question{A curve \( y = f(x) \) passes through \( (1, 3) \) and \( f'(x) = (2x + 1)(x - 3) \). Find \( f(x) \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Expand \( f'(x) \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
(2x+1)(x-3) = 2x^2 - 6x + x - 3 = 2x^2 - 5x - 3
\end{gathered}\]
FOIL the brackets.

\textit{Step 2: Integrate.}
\[\begin{gathered}
f(x) = \frac{2x^3}{3} - \frac{5x^2}{2} - 3x + C
\end{gathered}\]
Power rule applied to each term.

\textit{Step 3: Use the point \( (1, 3) \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
3 = \frac{2}{3} - \frac{5}{2} - 3 + C \implies C = 3 - \frac{2}{3} + \frac{5}{2} + 3 = 6 - \frac{4}{6} + \frac{15}{6} = 6 + \frac{11}{6} = \frac{47}{6}
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute \( x = 1 \), \( f(1) = 3 \) and solve for \( C \).

\textit{Step 4: Write the equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
f(x) = \frac{2x^3}{3} - \frac{5x^2}{2} - 3x + \frac{47}{6}
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute \( C = \dfrac{47}{6} \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  f(x) = \dfrac{2x^3}{3} - \dfrac{5x^2}{2} - 3x + \dfrac{47}{6} \)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Indefinite Integration 28\quad\small\texttt{(i1-028)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 28 (i1-028)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 5}

\question{A curve \( y = f(x) \) passes through \( (4, 9) \) and its gradient function is \( f'(x) = \sqrt{x} + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}} \). Find \( f(x) \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Rewrite in index notation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
f'(x) = x^{1/2} + x^{-1/2}
\end{gathered}\]
\( \sqrt{x} = x^{1/2} \) and \( \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}} = x^{-1/2} \).

\textit{Step 2: Integrate.}
\[\begin{gathered}
f(x) = \frac{x^{3/2}}{3/2} + \frac{x^{1/2}}{1/2} + C = \frac{2}{3}x^{3/2} + 2x^{1/2} + C
\end{gathered}\]
Apply the power rule to each term.

\textit{Step 3: Use the point \( (4, 9) \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
9 = \frac{2}{3}(8) + 2(2) + C = \frac{16}{3} + 4 + C
\end{gathered}\]
\( 4^{3/2} = 8 \) and \( 4^{1/2} = 2 \).

\textit{Step 4: Solve for \( C \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
C = 9 - \frac{16}{3} - 4 = 5 - \frac{16}{3} = \frac{15 - 16}{3} = -\frac{1}{3}
\end{gathered}\]
Rearrange.

\textit{Step 5: State the equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
f(x) = \frac{2}{3}x^{3/2} + 2\sqrt{x} - \frac{1}{3}
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute \( C = -\dfrac{1}{3} \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  f(x) = \dfrac{2}{3}x^{3/2} + 2\sqrt{x} - \dfrac{1}{3} \)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Indefinite Integration 29\quad\small\texttt{(i1-029)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 29 (i1-029)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{An object moves so that its acceleration at time \( t \) seconds is \( a = 6t - 2 \) ms\(^{-2}\). Given that the object is at rest when \( t = 0 \), find the velocity \( v \) as a function of \( t \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Velocity is the integral of acceleration.}
\[\begin{gathered}
v = \int (6t - 2) \, \mathrm{d}t = 3t^2 - 2t + C
\end{gathered}\]
Integrate with respect to \( t \).

\textit{Step 2: Use \( v = 0 \) when \( t = 0 \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
0 = 0 - 0 + C \implies C = 0
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute the initial condition.

\textit{Step 3: State the velocity function.}
\[\begin{gathered}
v = 3t^2 - 2t
\end{gathered}\]
No additional constant is needed.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  v = 3t^2 - 2t \)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Indefinite Integration 30\quad\small\texttt{(i1-030)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 30 (i1-030)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 5}

\question{An object has acceleration \( a = 10 - 4t \) ms\(^{-2}\). Given that the velocity is \( 8 \) ms\(^{-1}\) when \( t = 0 \), find: (a) The velocity function. (b) The time when the object reaches its maximum velocity.}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: (a) Integrate acceleration to find velocity.}
\[\begin{gathered}
v = \int (10 - 4t) \, \mathrm{d}t = 10t - 2t^2 + C
\end{gathered}\]
Power rule.

\textit{Step 2: Apply initial condition \( v(0) = 8 \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
8 = 0 + C \implies C = 8
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute \( t = 0 \), \( v = 8 \).

\textit{Step 3: State velocity function.}
\[\begin{gathered}
v = 10t - 2t^2 + 8
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute \( C = 8 \).

\textit{Step 4: (b) Maximum velocity when \( a = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t} = 0 \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
10 - 4t = 0 \implies t = 2.5 \text{ s}
\end{gathered}\]
Set the acceleration to zero.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad (a) \(\displaystyle  v = 10t - 2t^2 + 8 \) \textbackslash   (b) Maximum velocity at \(\displaystyle  t = 2.5 \) s
\end{answerbox}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int \left( \frac{x^3 + 2x^2 - x}{x^2} \right) \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Divide each numerator term by \( x^2 \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
x + 2 - x^{-1}
\end{gathered}\]
Splitting the fraction term-by-term gives a sum of powers of \( x \). Using index laws: \( \dfrac{x^3}{x^2} = x \), \( \dfrac{2x^2}{x^2} = 2 \), and \( \dfrac{-x}{x^2} = -x^{-1} \).

\textit{Step 2: Set up the integral.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int (x + 2 - x^{-1}) \, \mathrm{d}x
\end{gathered}\]
The reverse power rule \( \int x^n \, \mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C \) handles the \( x \) and the constant \( 2 \) directly, but it fails for \( x^{-1} \) because then \( n + 1 = 0 \) and we would divide by zero --- this is the famous \( n = -1 \) exclusion.

\textit{Step 3: Integrate, using the standard result \( \int x^{-1} \, \mathrm{d}x = \ln|x| \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
= \frac{x^2}{2} + 2x - \ln|x| + C
\end{gathered}\]
For the \( x^{-1} \) term we use the standard logarithm result \( \int \dfrac{1}{x} \, \mathrm{d}x = \ln|x| + C \) (the absolute value handles negative \( x \)). One \( +C \) covers the whole expression --- a single antiderivative family.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  \dfrac{x^2}{2} + 2x - \ln|x| + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 32\quad\small\texttt{(i1-032)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 32 (i1-032)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 6}

\question{A function \( f \) has gradient \( f'(x) = 3x^2 + kx - 4 \), where \( k \) is a constant. Given that \( f'(2) = 12 \) and the curve passes through \( (0, 5) \), find \( k \) and hence find \( f(x) \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Use \( f'(2) = 12 \) to find \( k \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
3(2)^2 + k(2) - 4 = 12 \implies 12 + 2k - 4 = 12 \implies 2k = 4 \implies k = 2
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute \( x = 2 \) into \( f'(x) \) and equate to the given gradient. This generates a linear equation in the unknown \( k \), which we then solve.

\textit{Step 2: Integrate \( f'(x) = 3x^2 + 2x - 4 \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
f(x) = \int (3x^2 + 2x - 4) \, \mathrm{d}x = x^3 + x^2 - 4x + C
\end{gathered}\]
Apply the reverse power rule \( \int x^n \, \mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C \) to each term: \( 3 \cdot \tfrac{x^3}{3} = x^3 \), \( 2 \cdot \tfrac{x^2}{2} = x^2 \), and \( \int -4 \, \mathrm{d}x = -4x \). The \( +C \) is essential because there is a whole family of antiderivatives that differ only by a constant.

\textit{Step 3: Use \( f(0) = 5 \) to pin down \( C \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
5 = (0)^3 + (0)^2 - 4(0) + C \implies C = 5
\end{gathered}\]
The boundary condition selects one specific antiderivative from the family. Substituting \( x = 0 \) makes every \( x \)-term vanish, so the equation reduces directly to \( C = 5 \).

\textit{Step 4: State the answer.}
\[\begin{gathered}
f(x) = x^3 + x^2 - 4x + 5
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute the found value \( C = 5 \) back into the general antiderivative to get the unique \( f(x) \) that satisfies both conditions.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  k = 2 \); \(\displaystyle  f(x) = x^3 + x^2 - 4x + 5 \)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Indefinite Integration 33\quad\small\texttt{(i1-033)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 33 (i1-033)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 5}

\question{The curve \( y = f(x) \) passes through \( (1, -1) \) and has \( f'(x) = (5x - 1)(x + 2) \). Find \( f(x) \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Expand \( f'(x) \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
(5x-1)(x+2) = 5x^2 + 10x - x - 2 = 5x^2 + 9x - 2
\end{gathered}\]
FOIL the brackets.

\textit{Step 2: Integrate.}
\[\begin{gathered}
f(x) = \frac{5x^3}{3} + \frac{9x^2}{2} - 2x + C
\end{gathered}\]
Apply the power rule.

\textit{Step 3: Use \( (1, -1) \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
-1 = \frac{5}{3} + \frac{9}{2} - 2 + C
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute \( x = 1 \).

\textit{Step 4: Solve for \( C \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
C = -1 - \frac{5}{3} - \frac{9}{2} + 2 = 1 - \frac{10}{6} - \frac{27}{6} = 1 - \frac{37}{6} = -\frac{31}{6}
\end{gathered}\]
Common denominator of 6.

\textit{Step 5: State the equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
f(x) = \frac{5x^3}{3} + \frac{9x^2}{2} - 2x - \frac{31}{6}
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute \( C = -\dfrac{31}{6} \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  f(x) = \dfrac{5x^3}{3} + \dfrac{9x^2}{2} - 2x - \dfrac{31}{6} \)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Indefinite Integration 34\quad\small\texttt{(i1-034)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 34 (i1-034)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 5}

\question{A curve \( y = f(x) \) has \( f'(x) = x^2 - \dfrac{4}{x^2} \) and passes through \( (2, 3) \). Find \( f(x) \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Rewrite \( \dfrac{4}{x^2} = 4x^{-2} \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
f'(x) = x^2 - 4x^{-2}
\end{gathered}\]
Index notation.

\textit{Step 2: Integrate.}
\[\begin{gathered}
f(x) = \frac{x^3}{3} - 4 \cdot \frac{x^{-1}}{-1} + C = \frac{x^3}{3} + \frac{4}{x} + C
\end{gathered}\]
Apply the power rule to each term.

\textit{Step 3: Use \( f(2) = 3 \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
3 = \frac{8}{3} + \frac{4}{2} + C = \frac{8}{3} + 2 + C
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute \( x = 2 \).

\textit{Step 4: Solve for \( C \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
C = 3 - \frac{8}{3} - 2 = 1 - \frac{8}{3} = -\frac{5}{3}
\end{gathered}\]
Rearrange.

\textit{Step 5: State the equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
f(x) = \frac{x^3}{3} + \frac{4}{x} - \frac{5}{3}
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute \( C = -\dfrac{5}{3} \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  f(x) = \dfrac{x^3}{3} + \dfrac{4}{x} - \dfrac{5}{3} \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 35\quad\small\texttt{(i1-035)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 35 (i1-035)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 7}

\question{A function \( f \) has gradient function \( f'(x) = 4x^3 + 3kx^2 + k \), where \( k \) is a constant. The curve \( y = f(x) \) passes through \( (1, 6) \) with gradient \( 12 \) at that point. (a) Find the value of \( k \). (b) Find \( f(x) \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: (a) Use the gradient condition \( f'(1) = 12 \) to set up an equation in \( k \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
f'(1) = 4(1)^3 + 3k(1)^2 + k = 4 + 3k + k = 4 + 4k
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute \( x = 1 \) into the gradient function and collect like terms. The unknown \( k \) survives because the two \( k \)-terms have the same sign, so they add rather than cancel.

\textit{Step 2: Set equal to 12 and solve.}
\[\begin{gathered}
4 + 4k = 12 \implies 4k = 8 \implies k = 2
\end{gathered}\]
A simple linear equation. Subtract 4 from both sides, then divide by 4.

\textit{Step 3: (b) Substitute \( k = 2 \) into \( f'(x) \) before integrating.}
\[\begin{gathered}
f'(x) = 4x^3 + 6x^2 + 2
\end{gathered}\]
Replacing the unknown constant first keeps the antiderivative computation tidy.

\textit{Step 4: Integrate using the reverse power rule.}
\[\begin{gathered}
f(x) = \int (4x^3 + 6x^2 + 2) \, \mathrm{d}x = x^4 + 2x^3 + 2x + C
\end{gathered}\]
Apply \( \int x^n \, \mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C \) to each term: \( 4 \cdot \tfrac{x^4}{4} = x^4 \), \( 6 \cdot \tfrac{x^3}{3} = 2x^3 \), and \( \int 2 \, \mathrm{d}x = 2x \). The \( +C \) is essential --- without a boundary condition the antiderivative is only known up to an additive constant.

\textit{Step 5: Use the point \( (1, 6) \) to pin down \( C \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
6 = (1)^4 + 2(1)^3 + 2(1) + C = 1 + 2 + 2 + C = 5 + C \implies C = 1
\end{gathered}\]
The boundary condition selects the one antiderivative whose graph actually passes through \( (1, 6) \) from the infinite family parametrised by \( C \).

\textit{Step 6: State the equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
f(x) = x^4 + 2x^3 + 2x + 1
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute \( C = 1 \) back into the general antiderivative.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad (a) \(\displaystyle  k = 2 \) \textbackslash   (b) \(\displaystyle  f(x) = x^4 + 2x^3 + 2x + 1 \)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Indefinite Integration 36\quad\small\texttt{(i1-036)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 36 (i1-036)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 1}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int 7x^2 \, \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Apply the power rule.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int 7x^2 \, \mathrm{d}x = 7 \cdot \frac{x^3}{3} + C = \frac{7x^3}{3} + C
\end{gathered}\]
Increase the index from 2 to 3 and divide by 3.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  \dfrac{7x^3}{3} + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 37\quad\small\texttt{(i1-037)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 37 (i1-037)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 2}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int (3x^2 + 4x - 1) \, \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Integrate term by term.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int (3x^2 + 4x - 1) \, \mathrm{d}x = x^3 + 2x^2 - x + C
\end{gathered}\]
Apply the reverse power rule \( \int x^n \, \mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C \) to each term: \( 3 \cdot \tfrac{x^3}{3} = x^3 \), \( 4 \cdot \tfrac{x^2}{2} = 2x^2 \), and integrating the constant \( -1 \) gives \( -x \). One \( +C \) covers the whole expression.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  x^3 + 2x^2 - x + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 38\quad\small\texttt{(i1-038)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 38 (i1-038)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 1}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int 10 \, \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{A constant integrates to the constant times \( x \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int 10 \, \mathrm{d}x = 10x + C
\end{gathered}\]
Think of \( 10 \) as \( 10x^0 \); the power rule increases the index from \( 0 \) to \( 1 \) and divides by \( 1 \), giving \( 10x \). The \( +C \) is required because every constant differentiates to zero, so all functions of the form \( 10x + C \) share the same derivative.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  10x + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Indefinite Integration 39\quad\small\texttt{(i1-039)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 39 (i1-039)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 2}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int x^{-3} \, \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Apply the power rule with \( n = -3 \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int x^{-3} \, \mathrm{d}x = \frac{x^{-2}}{-2} + C = -\frac{1}{2x^2} + C
\end{gathered}\]
Increase the index: \( -3 + 1 = -2 \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  -\dfrac{1}{2x^2} + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Indefinite Integration 40\quad\small\texttt{(i1-040)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 40 (i1-040)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 2}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int x^{\frac{1}{2}} \, \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Apply the power rule with \( n = \frac{1}{2} \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int x^{\frac{1}{2}} \, \mathrm{d}x = \frac{x^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\frac{3}{2}} + C = \frac{2}{3} x^{\frac{3}{2}} + C
\end{gathered}\]
Increase the index: \( \frac{1}{2} + 1 = \frac{3}{2} \). Dividing by \( \frac{3}{2} \) is the same as multiplying by \( \frac{2}{3} \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  \dfrac{2}{3} x^{\frac{3}{2}} + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 41\quad\small\texttt{(i1-041)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 41 (i1-041)}
\textit{Difficulty: Foundation \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 2}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int \left( 6x^5 - 2x + 3 \right) \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Integrate term by term.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int (6x^5 - 2x + 3) \, \mathrm{d}x = x^6 - x^2 + 3x + C
\end{gathered}\]
Apply the reverse power rule \( \int x^n \, \mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C \) to each term: \( 6 \cdot \tfrac{x^6}{6} = x^6 \), \( 2 \cdot \tfrac{x^2}{2} = x^2 \), and \( \int 3 \, \mathrm{d}x = 3x \). One \( +C \) covers the whole expression.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  x^6 - x^2 + 3x + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Indefinite Integration 42\quad\small\texttt{(i1-042)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 42 (i1-042)}
\textit{Difficulty: Standard \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 2}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int \frac{3}{x^4} \, \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Rewrite as a power of \( x \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
\frac{3}{x^4} = 3x^{-4}
\end{gathered}\]
Convert the fraction to a negative-index form so the power rule applies cleanly. The rule \( \int x^n \, \mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C \) works for any \( n \neq -1 \), including negative indices.

\textit{Step 2: Integrate.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int 3x^{-4} \, \mathrm{d}x = 3 \cdot \frac{x^{-3}}{-3} + C = -\frac{1}{x^3} + C
\end{gathered}\]
Increase the index from \( -4 \) to \( -3 \) and divide by \( -3 \). The two \( 3 \)s cancel, and dividing by a negative flips the sign --- a common spot for sign errors. Always include \( +C \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  -\dfrac{1}{x^3} + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 43\quad\small\texttt{(i1-043)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 43 (i1-043)}
\textit{Difficulty: Standard \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 2}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int 4\sqrt{x} \, \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Rewrite the surd as a fractional power.}
\[\begin{gathered}
4\sqrt{x} = 4x^{\frac{1}{2}}
\end{gathered}\]
Always convert surds to fractional powers before integrating --- the reverse power rule needs an explicit index \( n \). Here \( \sqrt{x} = x^{1/2} \).

\textit{Step 2: Apply the power rule.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int 4x^{\frac{1}{2}} \, \mathrm{d}x = 4 \cdot \frac{x^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\frac{3}{2}} + C = \frac{8}{3} x^{\frac{3}{2}} + C
\end{gathered}\]
Increase the index from \( \tfrac{1}{2} \) to \( \tfrac{3}{2} \) and divide by \( \tfrac{3}{2} \); dividing by a fraction is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal, so \( 4 \div \tfrac{3}{2} = 4 \times \tfrac{2}{3} = \tfrac{8}{3} \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  \dfrac{8}{3} x^{\frac{3}{2}} + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 44\quad\small\texttt{(i1-044)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 44 (i1-044)}
\textit{Difficulty: Standard \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 3}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int \left( x^3 - \frac{2}{x^2} \right) \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Rewrite using a negative index.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x^3 - \frac{2}{x^2} = x^3 - 2x^{-2}
\end{gathered}\]
Converting \( \dfrac{1}{x^2} = x^{-2} \) puts every term into the form \( x^n \), so the power rule applies directly.

\textit{Step 2: Integrate.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int (x^3 - 2x^{-2}) \, \mathrm{d}x = \frac{x^4}{4} + \frac{2}{x} + C
\end{gathered}\]
For \( x^3 \): increase the index to \( 4 \) and divide by \( 4 \). For \( -2x^{-2} \): the new index is \( -1 \), and dividing by \( -1 \) flips the sign giving \( -2 \cdot \dfrac{x^{-1}}{-1} = \dfrac{2}{x} \) --- watch the sign carefully.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  \dfrac{x^4}{4} + \dfrac{2}{x} + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 45\quad\small\texttt{(i1-045)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 45 (i1-045)}
\textit{Difficulty: Standard \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 3}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int \frac{x^3 + 2x}{x} \, \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Simplify the integrand by splitting the fraction.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\frac{x^3 + 2x}{x} = x^2 + 2
\end{gathered}\]
Divide each numerator term by \( x \): \( \dfrac{x^3}{x} = x^2 \) and \( \dfrac{2x}{x} = 2 \). Simplifying before integrating avoids any need for the quotient rule or other heavy machinery --- the power rule handles each term cleanly.

\textit{Step 2: Integrate term by term.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int (x^2 + 2) \, \mathrm{d}x = \frac{x^3}{3} + 2x + C
\end{gathered}\]
Apply the reverse power rule \( \int x^n \, \mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C \): the \( x^2 \) term becomes \( \tfrac{x^3}{3} \), and the constant \( 2 \) integrates to \( 2x \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  \dfrac{x^3}{3} + 2x + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 46\quad\small\texttt{(i1-046)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 46 (i1-046)}
\textit{Difficulty: Standard \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 3}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int \frac{6x^2 - 3}{x^2} \, \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Split the fraction term-by-term.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\frac{6x^2 - 3}{x^2} = 6 - 3x^{-2}
\end{gathered}\]
\( \dfrac{6x^2}{x^2} = 6 \) and \( \dfrac{-3}{x^2} = -3x^{-2} \). Writing the second term with a negative index puts it in the form \( x^n \) so the power rule can be applied.

\textit{Step 2: Integrate.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int (6 - 3x^{-2}) \, \mathrm{d}x = 6x + \frac{3}{x} + C
\end{gathered}\]
Integrating the constant \( 6 \) gives \( 6x \). For \( -3x^{-2} \): new index \( -1 \), divide by \( -1 \), giving \( -3 \cdot \dfrac{x^{-1}}{-1} = +\dfrac{3}{x} \) --- the two minus signs cancel, so be careful with the sign here.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  6x + \dfrac{3}{x} + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Indefinite Integration 47\quad\small\texttt{(i1-047)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 47 (i1-047)}
\textit{Difficulty: Standard \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 2}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int x^{-\frac{1}{2}} \, \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Apply the power rule.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int x^{-\frac{1}{2}} \, \mathrm{d}x = \frac{x^{\frac{1}{2}}}{\frac{1}{2}} + C = 2\sqrt{x} + C
\end{gathered}\]
\( -\frac{1}{2} + 1 = \frac{1}{2} \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  2\sqrt{x} + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 48\quad\small\texttt{(i1-048)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 48 (i1-048)}
\textit{Difficulty: Standard \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 3}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int \left( 2x + \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} \right) \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Rewrite the surd in index form.}
\[\begin{gathered}
2x + \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} = 2x + x^{-\frac{1}{2}}
\end{gathered}\]
Converting \( \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}} = x^{-1/2} \) puts the second term into a form the power rule can handle directly.

\textit{Step 2: Integrate term by term.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int \left(2x + x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) \mathrm{d}x = x^2 + 2x^{\frac{1}{2}} + C = x^2 + 2\sqrt{x} + C
\end{gathered}\]
For \( 2x \): the index becomes \( 2 \) and dividing by \( 2 \) cancels with the coefficient, giving \( x^2 \). For \( x^{-1/2} \): the new index is \( \tfrac{1}{2} \), and dividing by \( \tfrac{1}{2} \) doubles the term, giving \( 2\sqrt{x} \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  x^2 + 2\sqrt{x} + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 49\quad\small\texttt{(i1-049)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 49 (i1-049)}
\textit{Difficulty: Standard \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 3}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int (2x + 1)^2 \, \mathrm{d}x \) by expanding first.}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Expand the bracket.}
\[\begin{gathered}
(2x+1)^2 = 4x^2 + 4x + 1
\end{gathered}\]
Use \( (a+b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2 \) with \( a = 2x \), \( b = 1 \). You cannot integrate a bracket squared directly --- expand first so each term is a separate power of \( x \).

\textit{Step 2: Integrate term by term.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int (4x^2 + 4x + 1) \, \mathrm{d}x = \frac{4x^3}{3} + 2x^2 + x + C
\end{gathered}\]
Apply the reverse power rule to each term: \( 4 \cdot \tfrac{x^3}{3} = \tfrac{4x^3}{3} \), \( 4 \cdot \tfrac{x^2}{2} = 2x^2 \), and \( \int 1 \, \mathrm{d}x = x \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  \dfrac{4x^3}{3} + 2x^2 + x + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 50\quad\small\texttt{(i1-050)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 50 (i1-050)}
\textit{Difficulty: Standard \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 2}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int x(x - 3) \, \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Expand the bracket.}
\[\begin{gathered}
x(x-3) = x^2 - 3x
\end{gathered}\]
Multiply \( x \) through the bracket. The product of two algebraic expressions cannot be integrated termwise unless it is first expanded into a sum.

\textit{Step 2: Integrate.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int (x^2 - 3x) \, \mathrm{d}x = \frac{x^3}{3} - \frac{3x^2}{2} + C
\end{gathered}\]
Apply the reverse power rule to each term: \( \int x^2 \, \mathrm{d}x = \tfrac{x^3}{3} \) and \( \int -3x \, \mathrm{d}x = -3 \cdot \tfrac{x^2}{2} = -\tfrac{3x^2}{2} \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  \dfrac{x^3}{3} - \dfrac{3x^2}{2} + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 51\quad\small\texttt{(i1-051)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 51 (i1-051)}
\textit{Difficulty: Standard \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int \frac{x^2 + 4x + 3}{x + 1} \, \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Factorise the numerator and cancel.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\frac{x^2 + 4x + 3}{x + 1} = \frac{(x+1)(x+3)}{x+1} = x + 3
\end{gathered}\]
Find two numbers multiplying to \( 3 \) and adding to \( 4 \) --- namely \( 1 \) and \( 3 \). Cancelling the common factor \( (x+1) \) reduces the quotient to a simple linear expression, which the power rule can handle directly.

\textit{Step 2: Integrate.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int (x + 3) \, \mathrm{d}x = \frac{x^2}{2} + 3x + C
\end{gathered}\]
Apply the reverse power rule: \( \int x \, \mathrm{d}x = \tfrac{x^2}{2} \) and \( \int 3 \, \mathrm{d}x = 3x \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  \dfrac{x^2}{2} + 3x + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Indefinite Integration 52\quad\small\texttt{(i1-052)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 52 (i1-052)}
\textit{Difficulty: Standard \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 3}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int \sqrt{x}(x + 4) \, \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Expand by multiplying \( x^{1/2} \) through the bracket.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\sqrt{x}(x+4) = x^{\frac{3}{2}} + 4x^{\frac{1}{2}}
\end{gathered}\]
Use index laws: \( x^{1/2} \cdot x = x^{3/2} \) and \( x^{1/2} \cdot 4 = 4x^{1/2} \). Converting \( \sqrt{x} \) to \( x^{1/2} \) first lets the power rule apply cleanly after expansion.

\textit{Step 2: Integrate each fractional-index term.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int \left(x^{\frac{3}{2}} + 4x^{\frac{1}{2}}\right) \mathrm{d}x = \frac{2}{5}x^{\frac{5}{2}} + \frac{8}{3}x^{\frac{3}{2}} + C
\end{gathered}\]
For \( x^{3/2} \): new index \( \tfrac{5}{2} \), divide by \( \tfrac{5}{2} \) (i.e. multiply by \( \tfrac{2}{5} \)). For \( 4x^{1/2} \): new index \( \tfrac{3}{2} \), then \( 4 \times \tfrac{2}{3} = \tfrac{8}{3} \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  \dfrac{2}{5}x^{\frac{5}{2}} + \dfrac{8}{3}x^{\frac{3}{2}} + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\small The family of antiderivative curves \(y=F(x)+C\) --- vertical translates differing by the constant \(C\).\normalsize

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 53\quad\small\texttt{(i1-053)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 53 (i1-053)}
\textit{Difficulty: Standard \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{Given that \( \dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = 3x^2 - 4 \) and \( y = 5 \) when \( x = 2 \), find \( y \) in terms of \( x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Integrate the gradient function.}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = x^3 - 4x + C
\end{gathered}\]
Apply the reverse power rule: \( 3 \cdot \tfrac{x^3}{3} = x^3 \) and \( \int -4 \, \mathrm{d}x = -4x \). The \( +C \) is essential because integrating \( \tfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} \) recovers \( y \) only up to an additive constant.

\textit{Step 2: Use the condition \( y = 5 \) when \( x = 2 \) to find \( C \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
5 = (2)^3 - 4(2) + C = 8 - 8 + C \implies C = 5
\end{gathered}\]
The boundary condition pins down the value of \( C \), selecting one specific curve from the family of antiderivatives that all share the same gradient function.

\textit{Step 3: State the equation of the curve.}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = x^3 - 4x + 5
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute \( C = 5 \) back into the general antiderivative.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  y = x^3 - 4x + 5 \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 54\quad\small\texttt{(i1-054)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 54 (i1-054)}
\textit{Difficulty: Standard \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{The gradient of a curve is \( \dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = 6x - 1 \). The curve passes through \( (1, 4) \). Find the equation of the curve.}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Integrate the gradient function.}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = 3x^2 - x + C
\end{gathered}\]
Apply the reverse power rule: \( 6 \cdot \tfrac{x^2}{2} = 3x^2 \) and \( \int -1 \, \mathrm{d}x = -x \). The \( +C \) accounts for the infinite family of curves with the same gradient.

\textit{Step 2: Substitute the point \( (1, 4) \) to find \( C \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
4 = 3(1)^2 - 1 + C = 3 - 1 + C \implies C = 2
\end{gathered}\]
The boundary condition picks out the one curve in the family that actually passes through \( (1, 4) \).

\textit{Step 3: State the equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = 3x^2 - x + 2
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute \( C = 2 \) back into the general antiderivative.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  y = 3x^2 - x + 2 \)
\end{answerbox}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int \left( 5x^4 + \frac{3}{x^2} - 7 \right) \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Rewrite \( \tfrac{3}{x^2} \) as \( 3x^{-2} \) and integrate term by term.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int \left(5x^4 + 3x^{-2} - 7\right) \mathrm{d}x = x^5 - \frac{3}{x} - 7x + C
\end{gathered}\]
Converting to a negative index unlocks the power rule for the middle term. Integrating: \( 5 \cdot \tfrac{x^5}{5} = x^5 \); for \( 3x^{-2} \), new index \( -1 \) and dividing by \( -1 \) flips the sign to give \( -\tfrac{3}{x} \); and \( \int -7 \, \mathrm{d}x = -7x \). Watch the sign on the \( -\tfrac{3}{x} \) carefully.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  x^5 - \dfrac{3}{x} - 7x + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 56\quad\small\texttt{(i1-056)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 56 (i1-056)}
\textit{Difficulty: Standard \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int \frac{2x^4 - x^2 + 4}{x^2} \, \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Divide each term in the numerator by \( x^2 \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
\frac{2x^4 - x^2 + 4}{x^2} = 2x^2 - 1 + 4x^{-2}
\end{gathered}\]
Splitting the fraction term-by-term turns the awkward quotient into a sum of simple power-of-\( x \) terms, which the reverse power rule can handle directly. Note \( \dfrac{4}{x^2} = 4x^{-2} \) --- converting to a negative index is the key step that unlocks the power rule.

\textit{Step 2: Integrate using the reverse power rule.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int (2x^2 - 1 + 4x^{-2}) \, \mathrm{d}x = \frac{2x^3}{3} - x - \frac{4}{x} + C
\end{gathered}\]
Apply \( \int x^n \, \mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C \) term-by-term. For \( 4x^{-2} \): the new index is \( -1 \), and dividing by \( -1 \) flips the sign, giving \( -4x^{-1} = -\dfrac{4}{x} \). The \( +C \) is essential because indefinite integrals describe a whole family of antiderivatives.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  \dfrac{2x^3}{3} - x - \dfrac{4}{x} + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 57\quad\small\texttt{(i1-057)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 57 (i1-057)}
\textit{Difficulty: Standard \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 2}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int x^{\frac{2}{3}} \, \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Apply the power rule.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int x^{\frac{2}{3}} \, \mathrm{d}x = \frac{x^{\frac{5}{3}}}{\frac{5}{3}} + C = \frac{3}{5} x^{\frac{5}{3}} + C
\end{gathered}\]
Increase the index by \( 1 \): \( \tfrac{2}{3} + 1 = \tfrac{5}{3} \). Dividing by \( \tfrac{5}{3} \) is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal \( \tfrac{3}{5} \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  \dfrac{3}{5} x^{\frac{5}{3}} + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 58\quad\small\texttt{(i1-058)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 58 (i1-058)}
\textit{Difficulty: Standard \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 2}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int \frac{5}{\sqrt{x}} \, \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Rewrite the surd in index form.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\frac{5}{\sqrt{x}} = 5x^{-\frac{1}{2}}
\end{gathered}\]
Using \( \sqrt{x} = x^{1/2} \) and the reciprocal rule \( \dfrac{1}{x^{1/2}} = x^{-1/2} \). Putting the expression in the form \( kx^n \) is essential before applying the power rule.

\textit{Step 2: Integrate.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int 5x^{-\frac{1}{2}} \, \mathrm{d}x = 5 \cdot 2x^{\frac{1}{2}} + C = 10\sqrt{x} + C
\end{gathered}\]
Increase the index from \( -\tfrac{1}{2} \) to \( \tfrac{1}{2} \) and divide by \( \tfrac{1}{2} \), which is the same as multiplying by \( 2 \). Then \( 5 \times 2 = 10 \), and \( x^{1/2} = \sqrt{x} \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  10\sqrt{x} + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Indefinite Integration 59\quad\small\texttt{(i1-059)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 59 (i1-059)}
\textit{Difficulty: Standard \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 3}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int (x + 2)(x - 5) \, \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Expand the brackets.}
\[\begin{gathered}
(x+2)(x-5) = x^2 - 3x - 10
\end{gathered}\]
FOIL: \( x \cdot x - 5x + 2x - 10 = x^2 - 3x - 10 \). Expand before integrating --- the power rule applies to each individual power of \( x \), not to a product of brackets.

\textit{Step 2: Integrate term by term.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int (x^2 - 3x - 10) \, \mathrm{d}x = \frac{x^3}{3} - \frac{3x^2}{2} - 10x + C
\end{gathered}\]
Apply the reverse power rule: \( \int x^2 \, \mathrm{d}x = \tfrac{x^3}{3} \), \( \int -3x \, \mathrm{d}x = -\tfrac{3x^2}{2} \), and \( \int -10 \, \mathrm{d}x = -10x \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  \dfrac{x^3}{3} - \dfrac{3x^2}{2} - 10x + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\small The family of antiderivative curves \(y=F(x)+C\) --- vertical translates differing by the constant \(C\).\normalsize

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 60\quad\small\texttt{(i1-060)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 60 (i1-060)}
\textit{Difficulty: Standard \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{The gradient of a curve is \( \dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = 4x^3 + 2x \). The curve passes through \( (1, 0) \). Find the equation of the curve.}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Integrate the gradient function.}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = x^4 + x^2 + C
\end{gathered}\]
Apply the reverse power rule: \( 4 \cdot \tfrac{x^4}{4} = x^4 \) and \( 2 \cdot \tfrac{x^2}{2} = x^2 \). The \( +C \) is required because the gradient alone defines a whole family of parallel curves.

\textit{Step 2: Substitute \( (1, 0) \) to find \( C \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
0 = (1)^4 + (1)^2 + C = 1 + 1 + C \implies C = -2
\end{gathered}\]
The boundary condition selects the unique curve from the family that passes through this point.

\textit{Step 3: State the equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = x^4 + x^2 - 2
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute \( C = -2 \) into the general antiderivative.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  y = x^4 + x^2 - 2 \)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Indefinite Integration 61\quad\small\texttt{(i1-061)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 61 (i1-061)}
\textit{Difficulty: Standard \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 3}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int \left( 3\sqrt{x} - \frac{1}{x^3} \right) \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Rewrite in index form.}
\[\begin{gathered}
3\sqrt{x} - \frac{1}{x^3} = 3x^{\frac{1}{2}} - x^{-3}
\end{gathered}\]
Use \( \sqrt{x} = x^{1/2} \) and \( \dfrac{1}{x^3} = x^{-3} \). Putting every term as a power of \( x \) is essential before applying the power rule.

\textit{Step 2: Integrate each term.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int \left(3x^{\frac{1}{2}} - x^{-3}\right) \mathrm{d}x = 2x^{\frac{3}{2}} + \frac{1}{2x^2} + C
\end{gathered}\]
For \( 3x^{1/2} \): new index \( \tfrac{3}{2} \), and \( 3 \times \tfrac{2}{3} = 2 \). For \( -x^{-3} \): new index \( -2 \), divide by \( -2 \), giving \( -\dfrac{x^{-2}}{-2} = \dfrac{1}{2x^2} \) --- the two minus signs cancel.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  2x^{\frac{3}{2}} + \dfrac{1}{2x^2} + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 62\quad\small\texttt{(i1-062)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 62 (i1-062)}
\textit{Difficulty: Standard \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{Given \( f'(x) = 12x^2 - 6x + 1 \) and \( f(0) = 3 \), find \( f(x) \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Integrate the gradient function.}
\[\begin{gathered}
f(x) = 4x^3 - 3x^2 + x + C
\end{gathered}\]
Apply the reverse power rule: \( 12 \cdot \tfrac{x^3}{3} = 4x^3 \), \( 6 \cdot \tfrac{x^2}{2} = 3x^2 \), and \( \int 1 \, \mathrm{d}x = x \). The \( +C \) accounts for the unknown vertical shift.

\textit{Step 2: Use \( f(0) = 3 \) to pin down \( C \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
3 = 4(0)^3 - 3(0)^2 + 0 + C \implies C = 3
\end{gathered}\]
Substituting \( x = 0 \) makes every \( x \)-term vanish, so the boundary value goes straight to \( C \).

\textit{Step 3: State the final function.}
\[\begin{gathered}
f(x) = 4x^3 - 3x^2 + x + 3
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute \( C = 3 \) into the general antiderivative.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  f(x) = 4x^3 - 3x^2 + x + 3 \)
\end{answerbox}

\section*{Indefinite Integration 63\quad\small\texttt{(i1-063)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 63 (i1-063)}
\textit{Difficulty: Standard \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int \frac{(x+1)(x-1)}{x^2} \, \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Simplify using the difference of squares.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\frac{(x+1)(x-1)}{x^2} = \frac{x^2 - 1}{x^2} = 1 - x^{-2}
\end{gathered}\]
\( (x+1)(x-1) = x^2 - 1 \) by the difference of two squares. Then split the fraction: \( \dfrac{x^2}{x^2} = 1 \) and \( \dfrac{-1}{x^2} = -x^{-2} \). Putting it in this form lets the power rule apply to each term.

\textit{Step 2: Integrate.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int (1 - x^{-2}) \, \mathrm{d}x = x + \frac{1}{x} + C
\end{gathered}\]
\( \int 1 \, \mathrm{d}x = x \). For \( -x^{-2} \): new index \( -1 \), divide by \( -1 \), giving \( -\dfrac{x^{-1}}{-1} = +\dfrac{1}{x} \) --- the two negatives cancel, so the answer has a plus sign.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  x + \dfrac{1}{x} + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 64\quad\small\texttt{(i1-064)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 64 (i1-064)}
\textit{Difficulty: Standard \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 4}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int \left( x^2 + 1 \right)^2 \, \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Expand the bracket.}
\[\begin{gathered}
(x^2 + 1)^2 = x^4 + 2x^2 + 1
\end{gathered}\]
Use \( (a+b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2 \) with \( a = x^2 \), \( b = 1 \). The power rule cannot be applied to a bracket squared directly --- expand into a sum first.

\textit{Step 2: Integrate term by term.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int (x^4 + 2x^2 + 1) \, \mathrm{d}x = \frac{x^5}{5} + \frac{2x^3}{3} + x + C
\end{gathered}\]
Apply the reverse power rule to each term: \( \int x^4 \, \mathrm{d}x = \tfrac{x^5}{5} \), \( \int 2x^2 \, \mathrm{d}x = \tfrac{2x^3}{3} \), and \( \int 1 \, \mathrm{d}x = x \).

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  \dfrac{x^5}{5} + \dfrac{2x^3}{3} + x + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 65\quad\small\texttt{(i1-065)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 65 (i1-065)}
\textit{Difficulty: Standard \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 5}

\question{A curve has gradient function \( \dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{3}{x^2} + 2 \) and passes through \( (3, 10) \). Find \( y \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Rewrite \( \tfrac{3}{x^2} \) as \( 3x^{-2} \) and integrate.}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = \int (3x^{-2} + 2) \, \mathrm{d}x = -\frac{3}{x} + 2x + C
\end{gathered}\]
For \( 3x^{-2} \): new index \( -1 \), divide by \( -1 \) --- this flips the sign to give \( -\dfrac{3}{x} \). Then \( \int 2 \, \mathrm{d}x = 2x \). The \( +C \) is required since the gradient alone does not fix the curve uniquely.

\textit{Step 2: Substitute the point \( (3, 10) \) to find \( C \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
10 = -\frac{3}{3} + 2(3) + C = -1 + 6 + C \implies C = 5
\end{gathered}\]
The boundary condition selects the unique curve from the family that passes through \( (3, 10) \).

\textit{Step 3: State the equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = -\frac{3}{x} + 2x + 5
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute \( C = 5 \) into the general antiderivative.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  y = -\dfrac{3}{x} + 2x + 5 \)
\end{answerbox}

\small The family of antiderivatives (grey) with the particular solution (blue) through the given point.\normalsize

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 66\quad\small\texttt{(i1-066)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 66 (i1-066)}
\textit{Difficulty: Standard \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 3}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int \frac{x^4 - 1}{x^2} \, \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Split the fraction term-by-term.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\frac{x^4 - 1}{x^2} = x^2 - x^{-2}
\end{gathered}\]
\( \dfrac{x^4}{x^2} = x^2 \) and \( \dfrac{-1}{x^2} = -x^{-2} \). Writing the second term with a negative index unlocks the power rule.

\textit{Step 2: Integrate.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int (x^2 - x^{-2}) \, \mathrm{d}x = \frac{x^3}{3} + \frac{1}{x} + C
\end{gathered}\]
\( \int x^2 \, \mathrm{d}x = \tfrac{x^3}{3} \). For \( -x^{-2} \): new index \( -1 \), divide by \( -1 \), giving \( -\dfrac{x^{-1}}{-1} = +\dfrac{1}{x} \) --- the two minus signs cancel.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  \dfrac{x^3}{3} + \dfrac{1}{x} + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 67\quad\small\texttt{(i1-067)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 67 (i1-067)}
\textit{Difficulty: Standard \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 5}

\question{Find \( \displaystyle\int \left( \sqrt{x} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} \right)^2 \mathrm{d}x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Expand the bracket using \( (a+b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2 \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
\left(\sqrt{x} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\right)^2 = x + 2 + \frac{1}{x}
\end{gathered}\]
Here \( a^2 = (\sqrt{x})^2 = x \), \( b^2 = \dfrac{1}{x} \), and the middle term simplifies because \( 2 \cdot \sqrt{x} \cdot \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}} = 2 \). Expanding before integrating is essential --- the power rule cannot be applied directly to a bracket squared.

\textit{Step 2: Integrate term by term.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\int \left(x + 2 + x^{-1}\right) \mathrm{d}x = \frac{x^2}{2} + 2x + \ln|x| + C
\end{gathered}\]
Apply the reverse power rule to \( x \) and the constant \( 2 \), giving \( \tfrac{x^2}{2} \) and \( 2x \). The \( x^{-1} \) term is the special case \( n = -1 \) where the power rule fails (it would divide by zero), so we use the standard result \( \int \dfrac{1}{x} \, \mathrm{d}x = \ln|x| + C \) instead.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  \dfrac{x^2}{2} + 2x + \ln|x| + C \)
\end{answerbox}

\small The family of antiderivative curves \(y=F(x)+C\) --- vertical translates differing by the constant \(C\).\normalsize

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 68\quad\small\texttt{(i1-068)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 68 (i1-068)}
\textit{Difficulty: Standard \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 5}

\question{A curve passes through \( (4, 20) \) and has gradient \( \dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = 3\sqrt{x} \). Find the equation of the curve.}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Rewrite the surd and integrate.}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = \int 3x^{\frac{1}{2}} \, \mathrm{d}x = 3 \cdot \frac{2}{3} x^{\frac{3}{2}} + C = 2x^{\frac{3}{2}} + C
\end{gathered}\]
Convert \( \sqrt{x} = x^{1/2} \) so the power rule applies. Increase the index to \( \tfrac{3}{2} \) and divide by \( \tfrac{3}{2} \) (equivalently multiply by \( \tfrac{2}{3} \)); then \( 3 \times \tfrac{2}{3} = 2 \).

\textit{Step 2: Substitute the point \( (4, 20) \) to find \( C \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
20 = 2(4)^{\frac{3}{2}} + C = 2 \cdot 8 + C = 16 + C \implies C = 4
\end{gathered}\]
Use the identity \( 4^{3/2} = (\sqrt{4})^3 = 2^3 = 8 \). The boundary condition pins down which curve in the family passes through this point.

\textit{Step 3: State the equation.}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = 2x^{\frac{3}{2}} + 4
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute \( C = 4 \) into the general antiderivative.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  y = 2x^{\frac{3}{2}} + 4 \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 69\quad\small\texttt{(i1-069)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 69 (i1-069)}
\textit{Difficulty: Standard \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 5}

\question{Given \( f'(x) = 2x - \dfrac{4}{x^3} \) and \( f(1) = 3 \), find \( f(x) \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: Rewrite \( \tfrac{4}{x^3} \) as \( 4x^{-3} \) and integrate.}
\[\begin{gathered}
f(x) = \int (2x - 4x^{-3}) \, \mathrm{d}x = x^2 + \frac{2}{x^2} + C
\end{gathered}\]
For \( 2x \): \( 2 \cdot \tfrac{x^2}{2} = x^2 \). For \( -4x^{-3} \): new index \( -2 \), divide by \( -2 \), giving \( -4 \cdot \dfrac{x^{-2}}{-2} = +\dfrac{2}{x^2} \) --- the two minus signs cancel, so be careful with the sign.

\textit{Step 2: Substitute \( f(1) = 3 \) to find \( C \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
3 = (1)^2 + \frac{2}{(1)^2} + C = 1 + 2 + C \implies C = 0
\end{gathered}\]
The boundary condition gives \( C = 0 \), so no constant term is needed in the final function.

\textit{Step 3: State the final function.}
\[\begin{gathered}
f(x) = x^2 + \frac{2}{x^2}
\end{gathered}\]
Since \( C = 0 \), the antiderivative simplifies to this clean form.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad \(\displaystyle  f(x) = x^2 + \dfrac{2}{x^2} \)
\end{answerbox}

\medskip\hrule

\section*{Indefinite Integration 70\quad\small\texttt{(i1-070)}}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Indefinite Integration 70 (i1-070)}
\textit{Difficulty: Standard \quad\textbar\quad Marks: 7}

\question{A curve has second derivative \( \dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2 y}{\mathrm{d}x^2} = 6x \). The curve has a stationary point at \( (1, 2) \). (a) Find \( \dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} \). (b) Find \( y \) in terms of \( x \).}

\textbf{Worked solution.}

\textit{Step 1: (a) Integrate the second derivative to get the first derivative.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \int 6x \, \mathrm{d}x = 3x^2 + A
\end{gathered}\]
Apply the reverse power rule: \( 6 \cdot \tfrac{x^2}{2} = 3x^2 \). Use a different letter \( A \) for this constant of integration so it does not get confused with the constant from the second integration later.

\textit{Step 2: A stationary point means the gradient is zero, so use \( \tfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = 0 \) at \( x = 1 \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
0 = 3(1)^2 + A \implies A = -3
\end{gathered}\]
This boundary condition pins down \( A \), selecting the specific gradient function from the family of antiderivatives.

\textit{Step 3: State the gradient function.}
\[\begin{gathered}
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = 3x^2 - 3
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute \( A = -3 \) back into the general expression.

\textit{Step 4: (b) Integrate the gradient function to find \( y \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = \int (3x^2 - 3) \, \mathrm{d}x = x^3 - 3x + B
\end{gathered}\]
Apply the reverse power rule: \( 3 \cdot \tfrac{x^3}{3} = x^3 \) and \( \int -3 \, \mathrm{d}x = -3x \). A new constant \( B \) appears --- every integration introduces its own \( +C \).

\textit{Step 5: Use the point \( (1, 2) \) to find \( B \).}
\[\begin{gathered}
2 = (1)^3 - 3(1) + B = 1 - 3 + B \implies B = 4
\end{gathered}\]
The boundary condition selects the unique curve from the family that passes through \( (1, 2) \).

\textit{Step 6: State the equation of the curve.}
\[\begin{gathered}
y = x^3 - 3x + 4
\end{gathered}\]
Substitute \( B = 4 \) into the general antiderivative.

\begin{answerbox}
\textbf{Final answer:}\quad (a) \(\displaystyle  \dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = 3x^2 - 3 \) \textbackslash   (b) \(\displaystyle  y = x^3 - 3x + 4 \)
\end{answerbox}
